headline: Burnham signs post-Brexit reset package with the EU in Brussels

terms.meaning: The EU's shared trading area, where goods move with few checks or rules differences.
A scheme in which companies pay for the pollution they cause.
An agreement letting young people live and work in another country for a set time.

levels.headline: Burnham signs post-Brexit reset package with the EU in Brussels
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a post-Brexit reset package with the European Union at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. The government says the deals, covering food and agricultural standards, a link between carbon markets and a youth mobility scheme, are worth up to £17 billion a year, and could add up to 0.5% to GDP by 2040. That figure is the government's own estimate.
The food measures aim to cut paperwork and border checks on agricultural products. One report says the youth scheme would allow up to 100,000 young people from each side. Tuition fees, where a discounted-fee compromise is emerging, and access to the electricity market were left for later talks.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Britain would have to accept EU rules without a vote, calling it a betrayal. Mr Burnham said earlier that Brexit "has not worked" and promised a national conversation on the UK's long-term relationship with the EU. Labour's pledge not to rejoin the single market or customs union stands until the next election.
levels.why: It is the biggest change to the UK's relationship with the EU since Brexit and it is already dividing the parties.

levels.headline: Burnham signs post-Brexit reset package with the EU in Brussels
levels.body:
Andy Burnham signed a reset package with the EU in Brussels on 20 November. The government says it is worth up to £17 billion a year and could add up to 0.5% to GDP by 2040, though that is its own estimate.
The package covers food and agricultural standards, a link between the UK and EU carbon markets and a youth mobility scheme. The aim of the food deal is to cut paperwork and border checks. One report says up to 100,000 young people from each side could take part in the youth scheme.
Tuition fees and electricity market access were not settled. Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, said Britain would have to follow EU rules with no vote on them. Mr Burnham said Brexit has not worked and plans a national conversation about the long-term relationship. Labour's promise not to rejoin the single market or customs union lasts until the next election.
levels.why: It is the biggest change to the UK's relationship with the EU since Brexit and it is already dividing the parties.

levels.headline: Burnham signs post-Brexit reset package with the EU in Brussels
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has agreed a package of deals with the European Union at a summit in Brussels. The government says the deals could be worth up to £17 billion a year and add up to 0.5% to the size of the economy by 2040. This is the government's own estimate, not an independent one.
The deals cover food and farming rules, a link between carbon markets, which charge firms for pollution, and a scheme for young people to live and work abroad. Ministers say the food deal should cut checks at the border and ease pressure on supermarket prices.
Some questions remain open, including university fees for students and access to electricity markets. Reform UK's Nigel Farage said the deal means following EU rules without a say. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked and wants a national debate on the future relationship.
levels.why: It is the biggest change to the UK's relationship with the EU since Brexit and it is already dividing the parties.

levels.headline: Burnham agrees new deal with the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has struck a deal with the European Union in Brussels, which ministers say could be worth up to £17 billion a year to Britain. The government also says it could add up to 0.5% to the economy by 2040, but these are its own estimates.
The agreement makes it easier to trade food and farm products by cutting paperwork and checks at the border. It also links the UK and EU systems that charge companies for carbon pollution, and creates a scheme that lets young people live, work and travel on the other side.
Talks on university fees and electricity were left for later. Nigel Farage, who leads Reform UK, attacked the deal, saying Britain must accept EU rules with no vote. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked, and he plans a national conversation on what comes next.
levels.why: It is the biggest change to the UK's relationship with the EU since Brexit and it is already dividing the parties.

levels.headline: Burnham agrees new deal with the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has agreed a new deal with the EU, the group of countries next door to us. The government says it could be worth up to £17 billion a year to Britain. That is the government's own guess, so it may turn out differently.
The deal should make it simpler to sell food between Britain and Europe, because there will be less paperwork and fewer checks at the border. There will also be a scheme so that young people can live and work in other countries for a while. A separate part links the two sides' systems that make companies pay for pollution.
Not everything is agreed. Talks on university fees and electricity will carry on. Nigel Farage, a leading opponent, says Britain will have to follow EU rules without being able to vote on them. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked well enough.
levels.why: It could make some food cheaper and make travel and work in Europe easier for young people, though it also splits opinion.

levels.headline: Burnham agrees new deal with the EU
levels.body:
Britain and the European Union have agreed a new deal. Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed it in Brussels on 20 November. The government says it could be worth up to £17 billion a year, but that is only its own estimate.
The deal is about trade and travel. Food and farm goods should face fewer checks at the border, so there may be less paperwork for companies and perhaps lower prices in shops. Young people will be able to live and work in the EU for a while, and EU young people will be able to do the same here.
Not everything is settled yet. University fees and electricity are still being discussed. Some people, like Nigel Farage, dislike the deal. He says Britain will have to follow EU rules without a vote. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked and wants a big national conversation.
levels.why: It could make some food cheaper and make travel and work in Europe easier for young people, though it also splits opinion.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU agree to work more closely
levels.body:
The UK government has made a new deal with the European Union, a group of countries close to us. Britain left the EU some years ago, and since then trading with it has been harder. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, signed the new deal in Brussels. He says it could be worth up to £17 billion a year, but that is only a guess.
The deal should mean fewer checks on food at the border. That can make things cheaper to buy. Young people will also be able to live and work in Europe for a time. It also links the two sides' schemes that make companies pay for pollution.
Some things are not decided yet, like fees for students. Some politicians, such as Nigel Farage, do not like the deal. He says Britain must follow EU rules without a vote.
levels.why: It could make some food cheaper and make travel and work in Europe easier for young people, though it also splits opinion.

levels.headline: Britain and the EU agree to work more closely
levels.body:
The UK has made a deal with the European Union. The EU is a club of countries near us. Britain left it some years ago. Since then, trading with those countries has been harder.
The new deal should make some things easier. Food will face fewer checks when it crosses the border. That should save companies time and money, and it might help keep prices down in shops. Young people will also be allowed to live and work in Europe for a while.
The leader of the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, signed the deal. The government says it could be worth up to £17 billion a year, but nobody knows for sure. Some people, like Nigel Farage, do not like it. He says Britain will have to follow EU rules and will not get a vote on them. A few details are still being talked about.
levels.why: It is about how the UK and its closest neighbours work together, and it could change prices and chances for young people.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU make a new deal
levels.body:
Britain has made a new deal with the countries of the EU. The EU is a group of countries next to us. Britain left the group some years ago. Since then it has been harder to send things back and forth.
The new deal should help. Food will be checked less when it crosses the border. That means less waiting and less paperwork. It might make some things cheaper. Young people will also be able to live and work in Europe for a short time.
The Prime Minister is called Andy Burnham. He signed the deal. He thinks leaving the group did not work well. Some people disagree with him. One of them is Nigel Farage. He says Britain will have to follow the EU's rules and will not get a vote. Some parts of the deal are still being talked about.
levels.why: It is about how the UK and its closest neighbours work together, and it could change prices and chances for young people.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU make a new deal
levels.body:
Imagine your school and the school next door used to share a playground. Then your school said, "We will use our own playground." After that, it got harder to play together. You had to fill in forms and wait at the gate.
Now the two schools have made a new deal. The grown-up in charge of Britain, Andy Burnham, has agreed to share more things again. Food can go across the gate with fewer checks. Some young people will be able to visit and work in the other school's playground for a while.
Not everyone is happy. A man called Nigel Farage says it is not fair, because Britain will have to follow the other school's rules without a vote. A few things are still being talked about, so the grown-ups will keep chatting.
levels.why: It is about how the UK and its closest neighbours work together, and it could change prices and chances for young people.

headline: S&P 500 falls 3.7% to 6,910.39 as AI selloff pushes Wall Street into correction

terms.meaning: A fall of 10% or more from a recent high.
A US stock market index dominated by technology firms.
An index tracking 500 of the largest US companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls 3.7% to 6,910.39 as AI selloff pushes Wall Street into correction
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 20 November, the last completed session, falling 3.7% to 6,910.39. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% to 22,617.73, leaving it down about 2.7% for 2026. Trading Economics gave a slightly different Dow close of 48,034, so that figure varies by source.
The S&P 500 and Dow are now in correction territory, more than 10% below their record closes. Nvidia fell sharply after a Reuters report that the SEC is looking at its accounting. Over the week the Dow fell 8%, its worst since March 2020, the S&P 500 fell 8.6% and the Nasdaq about 10%.
CNBC linked the selloff to worries about the AI rally, including the Anthropic IPO, and about inflation. US stock futures pointed to a rebound of about 2% when trading resumed.
levels.why: It shows how much the value of American savings, pensions and big companies depends on the AI boom, and it affects markets worldwide.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply as the AI selloff deepens

Wall Street suffered a heavy fall on Friday 20 November, the last full session. The S&P 500 slid 3.7% to close at 6,910.39, the Dow lost 1.93% to finish at 48,147.33 and the Nasdaq plunged 5.28% to 22,617.73.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply as the AI selloff deepens
levels.body:

headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.
The group at the Bank that votes on interest rates.
One hundredth of a percentage point.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate, Bank Rate, by 0.25 percentage points to 4% on 5 November. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1 for the rise, with one member, Catherine Mann, voting for a larger rise of 0.5 points. It was the first increase since the Iran war began, according to CNBC.
The Bank said it expects UK inflation to rise to about 5% by the middle of 2027. It blamed mainly the conflict in the Middle East and higher energy prices.
CNBC reported that markets expect another rise at the 17 December meeting, with the implied chance falling to 80% from 90% after the latest inflation figures. Traders also price in further rises by June. The Bank's Financial Stability Report is due on 26 November.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer but can help savers, and the Bank expects prices to keep rising for months.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4% on 5 November. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1 in favour, and one member, Catherine Mann, wanted a bigger rise of 0.5 points. CNBC described it as the first rise since the Iran war began.
The Bank expects inflation to climb to about 5% by the middle of 2027. It pointed mainly to the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices as the cause.
After the October inflation figures, traders put the chance of another rise on 17 December at about 80%, down from 90%. Markets also expect more increases by June. The Bank publishes its Financial Stability Report on 26 November.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer but can help savers, and the Bank expects prices to keep rising for months.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. The Bank's rate-setting committee voted 8 to 1 for the change on 5 November. One member, Catherine Mann, wanted a bigger rise of half a percentage point.
The Bank puts up rates to slow price rises, because higher borrowing costs tend to cool spending. It now expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027, mainly because of the war in the Middle East and higher energy costs.
Financial markets expect another rise at the next meeting on 17 December, and more after that. For households, that can mean dearer mortgages and loans, but better returns for people with savings.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer but can help savers, and the Bank expects prices to keep rising for months.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%, up from 3.75%, in a bid to control rising prices. Its committee voted 8 to 1 on 5 November, with one member, Catherine Mann, arguing for a bigger half-point rise.
The Bank warned that inflation is likely to climb to about 5% by the middle of next year, largely because of the conflict in the Middle East and the effect on energy costs. Raising rates makes borrowing more expensive, which tends to slow spending and ease price rises.
Traders expect another rise on 17 December and several more by June. Borrowers with variable-rate mortgages or loans may soon pay more, while savers could earn a little more on their money.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer but can help savers, and the Bank expects prices to keep rising for months.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate to 4%. It was 3.75% before. The Bank does this to slow down rising prices. On 5 November, eight of the nine people who decide voted for the rise. The ninth, Catherine Mann, wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank thinks prices could rise by about 5% over a year by the middle of 2027. It says this is mostly because of the war in the Middle East, which has pushed up the price of energy.
When interest rates go up, loans and mortgages cost more to pay back. Savings can earn more. People in financial markets expect another rise in December. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments, savings and prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%. That is a small rise from 3.75%. The Bank is in charge of keeping prices steady. It raises rates when it thinks prices are going up too fast. Eight of the nine people who vote on this wanted the rise. One wanted an even bigger rise.
The Bank says prices could be going up by about 5% a year by the middle of next year. It says the main causes are the war in the Middle East and costly energy.
A higher interest rate means it costs more to borrow money, for example for a house. It also means savers may earn more. Many experts think there will be another rise on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments, savings and prices in the shops.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate to 4%. It was 3.75% before. The Bank does this when it wants prices to stop rising so fast. If it costs more to borrow money, people tend to spend a bit less, and shop prices rise more slowly. The vote was on 5 November. Eight people voted for the rise, and one, Catherine Mann, wanted a bigger one.
The Bank thinks prices could be rising by about 5% a year by the middle of 2027. It says the main reasons are the war in the Middle East and the cost of energy.
For families, a higher rate can mean bigger mortgage or loan payments. People who save may earn a little more. Many people expect another rise on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments, savings and prices in the shops.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates to 4%. An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. If you borrow, you pay a bit extra back. If you save, the bank pays you a bit extra. The Bank of England sets the main rate for the whole country.
It did this because prices are rising. That is called inflation. The Bank thinks prices might rise by about 5% in a year by next summer. It says the war in the Middle East has made energy cost more.
When the main rate goes up, mortgages and loans cost more. This can be hard for families. But savers can earn more. The Bank meets again on 17 December, and people expect another rise.
levels.why: It affects what families pay on loans and what savers earn.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England has made borrowing money more expensive. It put its main interest rate up to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The Bank of England is the place that sets the main rate for the country.
Why did it do that? Prices in shops have been going up. The Bank wants to slow that down. When borrowing costs more, people spend a little less, and prices rise more slowly. The Bank thinks a war far away is making energy cost more.
This can mean families pay more on loans. People with savings may get a bit more. The Bank will meet again on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects what families pay on loans and what savers earn.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow a pound from your friend for a week. Your friend says, "Give me back a pound and a penny." The extra penny is called interest. The Bank of England is a bit like the head of all the money in the country. It decides how big the extra penny should be.
This week the Bank made the extra penny bigger. It did this because things in shops cost more than before, and it wants to stop that. If borrowing costs more, people borrow and spend a bit less.
That can be hard for grown-ups who owe money. But it can be good for people who save, because they get a bit more. The Bank will check again in December.
levels.why: It affects what families pay on loans and what savers earn.

headline: UK inflation rises to a one-year high of 3.6% as record diesel prices bite

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of inflation.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which jump around a lot.
Petrol and diesel for vehicles.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to a one-year high of 3.6% as record diesel prices bite
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, a one-year high, according to figures released on 18 November. Motor fuel was the main driver, with fuel costs up 33.2% on a year earlier amid record diesel prices.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile items such as food and energy, held steady at 2.8%, and services inflation was 3.7%. The rise follows the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy prices.
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November and has warned that inflation could reach about 5% by the middle of 2027. After the figures, the market-implied chance of another rise on 17 December eased to 80% from 90%, though traders still expect several increases by June.
levels.why: Faster price rises squeeze household budgets and make further interest rate rises more likely.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to a one-year high of 3.6% as record diesel prices bite
levels.body:
UK inflation, measured by the Consumer Prices Index, rose to 3.6% in the year to October, a one-year high. Motor fuel prices were up 33.2% on a year earlier, helped by record diesel prices.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was steady at 2.8%. Services inflation stood at 3.7%. The Middle East conflict has been pushing energy prices higher.
The Bank of England lifted Bank Rate to 4% earlier this month and expects inflation to approach 5% by mid-2027. Following the data, traders cut the implied chance of a December rise to 80% from 90%, but still expect more increases by June.
levels.why: Faster price rises squeeze household budgets and make further interest rate rises more likely.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to a one-year high of 3.6% as record diesel prices bite
levels.body:
Prices across the UK rose by 3.6% in the year to October, the fastest pace in a year. The Consumer Prices Index is the main way of measuring this. The biggest cause was the cost of fuel, which was 33.2% higher than a year ago, with diesel prices at record levels.
A narrower measure, called core inflation, leaves out food and energy because they swing about. It stayed at 2.8%. Prices of services, such as haircuts and restaurant meals, rose 3.7%.
The war in the Middle East has pushed energy costs up. The Bank of England has already raised interest rates to 4% and thinks inflation could near 5% by the middle of next year. Markets still expect another rise in December.
levels.why: Faster price rises squeeze household budgets and make further interest rate rises more likely.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.6% on fuel costs
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, its highest level in a year, official figures showed. The main reason was fuel: the cost of petrol and diesel was 33.2% higher than a year before, with diesel at record prices.
The measure that leaves out food and energy, known as core inflation, was unchanged at 2.8%, while the rate for services was 3.7%. The conflict in the Middle East has driven up energy prices.
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4% and expects inflation to approach 5% by mid-2027. Investors reckon there is about an 80% chance of another rise in December, slightly lower than before the figures, and expect more increases by June.
levels.why: Faster price rises squeeze household budgets and make further interest rate rises more likely.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.6% on fuel costs
levels.body:
Prices in the UK went up faster in October. Inflation, which is how fast prices rise over a year, reached 3.6%. That is the highest for a year. The biggest reason was fuel. Petrol and diesel cost 33.2% more than a year ago, and diesel hit record prices.
Some prices rose more slowly. If you leave out food and energy, which change a lot, inflation was 2.8%. The price of services, like getting your hair cut, went up 3.7%.
The war in the Middle East has made energy more expensive. The Bank of England has put up interest rates to 4% to slow prices down. It thinks inflation could reach about 5% by the middle of next year.
levels.why: Higher prices mean money buys less, especially when filling up a car.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.6% on fuel costs
levels.body:

headline: European leaders reject 'Yalta 2.0' for Ukraine after Trump meets Putin and Xi

levels.headline: European leaders reject 'Yalta 2.0' for Ukraine after Trump meets Putin and Xi
levels.body:
European leaders have rejected what commentators called a "Yalta 2.0" approach to the war in Ukraine after US President Donald Trump met Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on 19 November, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Their joint statement, the "Declaration Toward Peace", did not mention Ukraine. The name refers to the 1945 Yalta conference, where great powers shaped postwar Europe.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a Yalta format would not bring peace, and France's Emmanuel Macron said Europe should be part of any talks. At a Berlin meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, leaders agreed Europe should engage in face-to-face negotiations with Russia and named a seven-member team. Mr Putin said Europeans should come to Moscow.
Mr Trump, joining the Berlin meeting by phone, asked why allies keep spending billions on Kyiv. Envoy Jared Kushner said the US was open to an Article 5-style guarantee for Ukraine. Euronews analysis found no breakthrough on Ukraine.
levels.why: The meeting raised fears that big powers might decide Europe's future without Europeans, with a war still under way in Ukraine.

headline: COP31 climate talks end without a deal after EU rejects text that omits fossil fuels

levels.headline: COP31 climate talks end without a deal after EU rejects text that omits fossil fuels
levels.body:
The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on 22 November without an agreed deal, after talks ran two days past their scheduled finish and became the longest UN climate conference on record. COP31 President Murat Kurum said there was no consensus and the decisions were not adopted.
The sticking point was fossil fuels. An early draft called for a faster phase-out, but a later version removed all mention of them. The final text kept a goal to electrify the global economy and a push for carbon capture without naming fossil fuels. The EU and Panama rejected it, with Ireland's O'Brien, speaking for the EU presidency, saying the bloc would not endorse a text that did not mention fossil fuels.
Observers said Saudi Arabia and other big oil producers pushed to keep explicit fossil fuel language out. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was deeply disappointed.
levels.why: Without agreement, there is no new shared plan on cutting the fossil fuels that drive climate change.

headline: Treasury yields fall as investors seek safety and Nvidia drops 14% on reported SEC probe

terms.meaning: The return on US government bonds, which moves opposite to bond prices.

levels.headline: Treasury yields fall as investors seek safety and Nvidia drops 14% on reported SEC probe
levels.body:
US government bond yields fell sharply on Friday 20 November as investors fled to safe havens during the stock selloff. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped 12 basis points to 4.932%, and the 2-year and 30-year yields also fell. The move back below 5% was notable because the 10-year yield had risen above that level after the Federal Reserve skipped a rate rise in late October.
LPL Financial's Lawrence Gillum said the safe-haven bid was clearly alive and well. Yields move in the opposite direction to bond prices, so falling yields mean rising demand.
Nvidia shares fell about 14% after Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking at the chipmaker's accounting, a report not confirmed by the agency. California's attorney general, Rob Bonta, has also sent a subpoena asking whether its advanced chips reached China.
levels.why: It shows investors moving from risky shares to safer government bonds, which can change borrowing costs worldwide.

headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.6% and retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.6% and retail sales volumes rise 0.7% in October
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate fell to 4.6%, down 0.3 percentage points on both the year and the quarter, according to the Office for National Statistics, in figures published on 17 November.
Separately, the ONS estimates that retail sales volumes rose 0.7% in October, following a 0.6% fall in September, which was revised down from an earlier estimate of a 0.4% fall. Over the three months to October, volumes were up 0.4%. The next retail sales release is due on 18 December.
The figures come as inflation has risen to 3.6% and the Bank of England has raised Bank Rate to 4%, so shoppers and households face higher prices and borrowing costs. Volumes measure the amount bought after stripping out the effect of price rises, so they show real changes in spending rather than higher prices.
levels.why: Jobs and shop spending show how households are coping as prices and interest rates rise.
